sn12.4:1.2: In early texts, Vipassī is invariably mentioned along with the full group of seven Buddhas ([thag7.5](), [dn32:3.2](), [pli-tv-bu-vb-pj1:3.1.6]()). Their details are given in the Mahāpadāna Sutta ([dn14]()). There, the story of Vipassī is recounted in full; the key doctrinal passages are shared with the current discourse ([dn14:2.18.5]()). | _Bodhisatta_ is explained by the commentary here as either “one possessed of awakening”, or one who is certain of awakening in the proximity of Buddhahood. The latter explanation allows a reading equivalent to Sanskrit _bodhiśakta_ (“one intent on awakening”), rather than the more familiar _bodhisattva_ (“awakening-being”).
sn12.4:2.2: This phrasing corresponds to the abstract principle of dependent origination ([sn12.37:2.2]()). Compare Śaunaka’s question at Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.3:  “When what is understood, sir, is all this understood?” (_kasmin nu bhagavo vijñāte sarvaṁ idaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati_).
sn12.4:2.3: _Yoniso maniskāra_ (“rational application of mind”) is a distinctively Buddhist term that literally means “applying the mind by way of source”. It is mostly used in investigating causality, although over time it came to have a more general sense of “reflection, inquiry, attention”.
sn12.4:11.4: Here we have the normal twelve links, whereas in DN 14 the sequence omits ignorance and choices, emphasizing rather the mutual interdependence of consciousness with name and form, a variation found also in the context of Gotama’s awakening at [sn12.65]().
sn12.4:25.4: This phrasing recalls the Buddha’s first sermon ([sn56.11:5.1]()), an insight that is said to be common to all Buddhas ([sn56.12:1.1]()). | _Pubbe ananussutesu_ (“not learned before from another”) means that this is a fresh insight not passed down in an oral tradition.
sn12.4:26.1: This instruction is noted in the Pali text.
